summary:
Sections 365 and 365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity. Section 365 covers "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and has been applied to men; Section 365A covers "gross indecency" and was amended in 1995 to reach women, so both provisions now apply to men and women. The maximum penalty is ten years' imprisonment. Where an offence under these sections is committed by a person over 18 against a person under 16, the penalty rises to ten to twenty years' rigorous imprisonment.

Prosecutions are limited. The Canada Immigration and Refugee Board's January 2012 research found no convictions under the articles, and Outright International's March 2026 overview describes prosecutions as limited. The provisions nonetheless structure everyday policing. The US State Department's country report documents police harassment of LGBT persons, and the 2012 research found that criminalisation "paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to brand all lesbian, bisexual, transgendered persons as perverts and criminals". Outright International records frequent harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services. Advocacy groups report that police routinely ignore complaints from LGBTQ victims, particularly those involving sexual violence or blackmail, citing Article 365 as justification, and human rights organisations have documented police using the threat of arrest to assault, harass and extort LGBTQIA individuals. Article 365 remains cited to justify police harassment and moral policing of LGBTQ people in public and private settings.

An August 2023 opinion piece published by the International Commission of Jurists, by Mathuri Thamilmaran, states that the Sri Lanka Police are the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals, and that both the Police and the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka acknowledged this in the preceding months. The piece argues that administrative circulars cannot substitute for legal reform.

Outright International reports that authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence, a practice widely condemned as torture.

No comprehensive anti-discrimination protections exist.

Legal gender recognition is available through a certification process. In 2016 the Ministry of Health issued a circular to health services and education institutions on issuing gender recognition certificates to transgender people, following a March 2015 complaint facilitated by the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka. No surgical intervention is legally required, though the certification is bureaucratic and may be onerous to obtain.

Gender-affirming surgery is relatively inaccessible. Many hospitals lack the specialised surgical units and staff required, and a physician interviewed for Human Rights Watch's 2016 report said Sri Lankan doctors were often unfamiliar with surgical treatment for transgender patients. Patients report ignorance, curiosity and ridicule from medical staff when seeking gender-confirming care, and some avoid public hospitals and clinics as a result, which raises their treatment costs. Obtaining hormone therapy is described as similarly fraught.

The National Blood Transfusion Service bars men who have anal sex with men from donating blood, classifying male same-sex intercourse as "risky behaviour" alongside drug use and having multiple partners.

Family law does not recognise same-sex marriage or same-sex civil unions and gives no equal rights to same-sex live-in couples; the marriage law dates from colonial times and is based on European law. A trans visitor whose relationship is read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to marriage or civil-union recognition and no equal rights as a live-in partner.
tangentialFactors:
Public reference coverage characterises Sri Lankan society as generally tolerant of homosexuality; polling gives a more mixed picture. A 2021 Social Scientists Association poll found 72.5% believed LGBT people should not be punished for their sexual identity, 65% said an LGBT person can do a job as well as anyone else, and 51.4% would support rights legislation. A 2023 report found 69% of the population opposed legalising same-sex unions, with 60% strongly opposed. A 2018 Equality Fund survey found 12% of respondents were LGBTQI.

Political signals are mixed. In March 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa tweeted that he was determined to secure everybody's right to live with dignity regardless of sexuality and gender, which the Financial Times described as the first such public acknowledgement by a South Asian head of state. Politicians from both major parties and across the spectrum have expressed support for LGBTQ rights, and the influential Asgiriya Buddhist chapter has backed rights extension and constitutional amendment. The Catholic Church in Sri Lanka does not recognise same-sex marriages; Cardinal Malcolm Ranjith has stated that same-sex marriages "are not a human right".

Conversion therapy is unregulated in practice. In August 2021 a video of a homophobic counsellor caused controversy, and the College of Psychiatrists clarified that modern medicine does not consider homosexuality an illness and called for decriminalisation, noting that counsellors, unlike psychiatrists, are not regulated and do not require degrees. In March 2022 SJB MP Rohini Kumari Wijerathna tabled a bill to ban conversion therapy, which she said the government had failed to support as of July 2024. Despite professional college ethics, doctors are reportedly still regularly sought by families to administer "treatment" to LGBTQ members.

Two documentation sources frame the country's record. A joint stakeholder report for Sri Lanka's third universal periodic review cycle, submitted by EQUAL GROUND, Northwestern CIHR and GIHR, documents criminalisation and violations. The UK Home Office's September 2024 country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression assesses risk from state and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims.
localsOnly:
Prisons have no dedicated transgender housing. In October 2024 the Prisons Department's media spokesperson and Commissioner, Gamini Dissanayake, said current facilities make separate space for transgender prisoners impossible and that separate accommodation is planned only for prisons built in the future. Placement is decided case by case: detainees holding the recognised identity card issued under the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular are accommodated according to their preferred gender "where possible", while those without it undergo a doctor's assessment of whether they "can be considered a transgender", with the inmate's preference weighed in the decision. Officials have stated that they worry about people accused of sex offences "identifying as transgender" to enter female housing with born-male offenders, which they give as a reason for resisting gender-based placement. The practical default in the current male and female ward system is placement by birth sex, with a medicalised discretionary exception and no statutory placement rule. The Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners has asked that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate space of their own choosing, including possible space within prison hospitals.

Community organisations include Companions on a Journey, founded in 1994 as the country's first LGBTQ support group, the Women's Support Group (1999) and Equal Ground.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Sri Lanka was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403). Its documented finding that the penal code criminalises same-sex activity is consistent with the sources above but could not be verified directly.

Whether the 2016 gender recognition certification process is open to foreign nationals is not addressed in the sources reviewed, and no local gender marker document available to a visitor is identified.

No youth-specific findings on access to gender-affirming care appear in the source material.

Conviction data under Sections 365 and 365A rests on the January 2012 Immigration and Refugee Board finding of no convictions; no more recent conviction figures were located.

The status of the March 2022 conversion therapy bill after July 2024 is not sourced.

Prison placement for transgender detainees remains uncodified; no statutory rule or published policy was identified.
